section_summary: This section documents Japanese military activity and authority in Manchuria and China from 1934 to 1938. It begins with diplomatic correspondence over pressure on foreign firms to finance Dairen’s air defenses, followed by a report on a citywide blackout exercise. Later documents analyze the Kwantung Army’s autonomy, finances, recruitment plans, and relationship with Tokyo, and report rumors of its reorganization; the final telegram concerns military-training films requested by the Kwangtung provincial authorities in Canton.

subfiles.title: Foreign Firms Requested to Contribute towards Air Defense of Dairen
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the Dairen authorities’ solicitation of substantial foreign-business contributions for air-defense maneuvers and equipment.
subfiles.summary: Dairen's mayor's Air Defense Contribution Committee assessed foreign firms, including ¥3,000 from two banks and ¥2,000 from Standard-Vacuum; managers found them excessive and feared retaliation but mostly agreed to ignore the letter.

subfiles.title: Translated Contribution Request from the Dairen Air Defense Contribution Committee
subfiles.from: J. Ogawa, chairman, Dairen Air Defense Contribution Committee
subfiles.about: Requests a designated contribution toward urban air-defense preparations.
subfiles.summary: Translated form letter from the Dairen Air Defense Contribution Committee congratulating the recipient and asking compliance with the assessed contribution, citing the crisis and urban air defense.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 126 Requesting the Status of the Dairen Contributions
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Orders the Embassy to determine the current status of Dairen’s solicitation of foreign firms.
subfiles.summary: Telegram 126 asks the Embassy to get Vincent's update on his June 29 despatch on air-defense contributions.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 74 on Possible Compulsion and Treaty Infringement
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Considers whether fear of retaliation made Dairen’s donation requests incompatible with the 1911 treaty.
subfiles.summary: Grew: coercive contribution requests might violate Article I of the 1911 treaty; he awaits evidence of compulsion and asks Vincent for an update.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 164 on the Second Ogawa Letter
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports a renewed request for donations and asks whether Japan should be approached about possible treaty implications.
subfiles.summary: Vincent: foreign firms got another mayoral letter near the deadline but none will respond and no compulsion occurred; Grew argues fear of retaliation contravenes the 1911 treaty and seeks instructions.

subfiles.title: Instructions to Protest the Dairen Mayor’s Action
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State
subfiles.about: Directs the Embassy to seek Japanese disavowal of the Dairen mayor’s contribution campaign.
subfiles.summary: Department tells the Embassy to speak orally to the Foreign Minister, citing Article I of the 1911 treaty and asking measures against reprisals; Vincent to tell American firms to report retaliation.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 171 Reporting Oral Representations
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports that the Embassy protested the Dairen solicitation and that local anxiety had diminished.
subfiles.summary: Grew made oral representations August 1 and awaits a reply; Vincent says Dairen foreign managers see less danger of retaliation.

subfiles.title: Telegram No. 186 Reporting Japanese Disavowal
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Grew, American Embassy, Tokyo
subfiles.about: Reports the Japanese Government’s rejection of compulsory foreign contributions for Dairen air defense.
subfiles.summary: Vice Minister told Grew the Government disapproved the mayor's action; Kwantung's governor ordered contributions from foreigners neither exacted nor expected; no indirect pressure or retaliation.

subfiles.title: Further Report on Contributions toward Dairen Air Defense
subfiles.from: John Carter Vincent, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Transmits the mayor’s renewed letter and identifies the American firms that received it.
subfiles.summary: Vincent: Ogawa's July 20 letter reached foreign firms shortly before the July 31 deadline, the committee seeking ¥700,000; American recipients were Standard-Vacuum and National City Bank, assessed ¥2,000 and ¥3,000.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference to Grew’s Report on Dairen Contributions
subfiles.from: Department of State records staff
subfiles.about: Directs researchers to another file for Grew’s report on the Dairen mayor’s request.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: report 917 of August 4, 1934 on the mayor's request that foreign firms contribute to Dairen air defense (894.00 P.R./80).

subfiles.title: Request of the Mayor of Dairen that Foreign Firms Contribute Financially toward Air Defense
subfiles.from: U.S. Department of State, author not stated
subfiles.about: Summarizes the Dairen contribution controversy and the American treaty-based protest.
subfiles.summary: Memo: most American firms refused the mayor's requests but feared retaliation; quotes the 1911 treaty's exemptions from forced loans and military exactions and the Embassy's request that Japan disavow the mayor.

subfiles.title: Practice for the Air Defense of Dairen
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Grew, American Ambassador at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Describes a highly effective citywide blackout during a simulated air raid.
subfiles.summary: During thirtieth-anniversary celebrations of the Russo-Japanese War, Dairen staged a nighttime air-raid exercise with nearly all lights out for ten minutes, which Grummon saw as striking discipline; another set for March 11.

subfiles.title: Handwritten Routing Note concerning an FE Copy for MID
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs, author not legible
subfiles.about: Suggests lending or forwarding the Far Eastern Affairs copy of a report to Military Intelligence.
subfiles.summary: Fragmentary handwritten note recommending lending FE's copy to MID, noting other copies may be destroyed; report unidentified.

subfiles.title: Request from MID for Mukden Report No. 264
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Records a Military Intelligence Division request to see Mukden’s report no. 264.
subfiles.summary: The note says that Miss Van Lyne of MID telephoned seeking report no. 264 from Mukden, identified there as dated May 12, 1936 and filed under 894C.20/10. It asks whether a copy should be sent to MID and includes a Communications and Records routing page dated September 23.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on Peiping Despatch No. 474 and the Kwantung Army
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes and critically evaluates reports about the Kwantung Army’s autonomy and long-term plans.
subfiles.summary: Memo on Peiping Despatch 474: the Kwantung Army dominated Manchukuo and sought financial and recruiting autonomy via taxes, a permanent garrison and immigration; the writer doubts it was independent of Tokyo or that Manchukuo could be self-sufficient.

subfiles.title: The Kwantung Army: Covering Despatch No. 474
subfiles.from: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Embassy, Peiping
subfiles.about: Transmits Mukden despatch no. 264 on the Kwantung Army’s relations with Manchukuo and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Johnson encloses the May 13 Mukden consulate report on trends affecting the Kwantung Army's position relative to Manchukuo and Japan.

subfiles.title: The Kwantung Army
subfiles.from: Joseph W. Ballantine, American Consul General at Mukden
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Ambassador at Peiping
subfiles.about: Analyzes the Kwantung Army’s control of Manchukuo, its degree of independence from Tokyo, and its plans for financial and military self-sufficiency.
subfiles.summary: Ballantine describes the Kwantung Army’s control of Manchukuo through liaison between its Third Staff Section and the General Affairs Board, while portraying its commander as formally responsible to the Emperor and only loosely constrained by Tokyo. He argues that declining military prestige after the February 26 Incident and Japanese resentment of Manchurian expenditures could threaten the army’s position. Projects intended to reduce that vulnerability included taxing Japanese residents, improving revenue collection and trade, creating a permanent local garrison, and settling large numbers of Japanese households to supply recruits. He concludes that a locally financed and recruited Kwantung Army could resist policy changes in Japan and profoundly alter relations between Manchukuo, the army, and the home forces.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference: Relation of the Kwantung Army to the South Manchuria Railway Company
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, Dairen
subfiles.about: Points to another file for a despatch on the Kwantung Army’s relationship with the South Manchuria Railway Company.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Grummon's June 19, 1936 Dairen despatch on the Kwantung Army and the South Manchuria Railway Company (894C.77/24).

subfiles.title: Instance of Difference of Viewpoint between the Kwantung Army and Tokyo War Ministry
subfiles.from: Stuart E. Grummon, American Consul at Dairen
subfiles.to: Edwin L. Neville, American Chargé d’Affaires ad interim at Tokyo
subfiles.about: Uses the obstruction of a British air attaché’s tour to illustrate local Kwantung Army independence from Tokyo.
subfiles.summary: Commander Chappelle had War Ministry permission to inspect Manchurian airports but local military blocked visits to Heiho and Kungchuling and denied a reserved flight; Grummon sees Kwantung independence from Tokyo.

subfiles.title: Departmental Summary of Rumored Kwantung Army Reorganization
subfiles.from: Division of Far Eastern Affairs
subfiles.about: Summarizes Mukden rumors of changes intended to give Tokyo greater control over Japanese continental forces.
subfiles.summary: Departmental summary of rumors that General Terauchi might replace Ueda, or the Kwantung Army would lose its identity inside a continental high command, probably under Terauchi.

subfiles.title: Change in the Kwantung Army: Covering Despatch
subfiles.from: John Davies, Jr., American Vice Consul at Mukden
subfiles.about: Transmits a confidential report on rumors of a change in the Kwantung Army.
subfiles.summary: Davies encloses despatch 200 to Peiping on possible changes in the Kwantung Army's organization or command.

subfiles.title: Change in the Kwantung Army
subfiles.from: John Davies, Jr., American Vice Consul at Mukden
subfiles.to: Nelson Trusler Johnson, American Ambassador at Peiping
subfiles.about: Reports competing rumors about the replacement of General Ueda and creation of a unified Japanese continental command.
subfiles.summary: Sources said Ueda would return to Japan and Terauchi replace him, or the Kwantung Army be absorbed into a high command over forces in China and Manchukuo; all attributed it to stronger Tokyo control.

subfiles.title: Cross-Reference to Telegram on Military-Training Films
subfiles.from: Department of State records staff
subfiles.about: Points to the films file for Linnell’s telegram about training films requested by Kwangtung authorities.
subfiles.summary: Cross-reference: Linnell's July 19 Canton telegram on films for recruit education (102.Films/165).

subfiles.title: Telegram Requesting Military-Training Films for Kwangtung Recruits
subfiles.from: Linnell, Canton
subfiles.about: Requests information about obtaining films on modern military operations and equipment for Kwangtung recruit training.
subfiles.summary: Kwangtung Governor's office asks for films to train Citizens Military Training recruits on aircraft, air defense, guns, tanks, poison gas and bridges; Linnell asks if they can be loaned or rented.
